day.description: Computer use CLI for AI agents
day.readme: Computer use for AI agents: read and operate desktop apps through the OS accessibility tree. A CLI and C library for macOS, Windows and Linux. A snapshot returns JSON with a ref for every element an agent can act on. The agent acts on a ref and snapshots again to check, with no pixel matching; the loop stays in your agent. day.description: Worktrunk is a CLI for Git worktree management, designed for parallel AI agent workflows
day.readme: Worktrunk is a CLI for git worktree management, designed for running AI agents in parallel. Worktrunk's three core commands make worktrees as easy as branches. Plus, Worktrunk has a bunch of quality-of-life features to simplify working with many parallel changes, including hooks to automate local workflows & copy-on-write build caches. AI agents like Claude Code and Codex can handle longer tasks without supervision, such that it's possible to manage 5-10+ in parallel.

day.description: A hierarchical inference engine for frontier MoE models: hot experts on the GPU (CUDA, Vulkan), warm ones in RAM, cold ones streamed from NVMe. Written in C, runs on the hardware you already own.
day.readme: Tiny engine, immense model. colibri runs very large open models on the machine you already have. A mixture-of-experts model of hundreds of billions of parameters uses only a small part of itself for each token, so colibri keeps that part in RAM and reads the rest, the experts, from the disk when the model asks for them. Pure C, one file per model family, no GPU required. Thirteen engines run today.

These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy.

new.readme: Install Linux next to Windows without a USB stick. hop is a single Windows app that installs Linux alongside Windows. new.description: Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LuaLaTeX, drawn in Lua
new.readme: asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made. This project is one possible way, and the way I did it uses hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua and placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original.

threats.title: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys compromised
threats.headline: Flawed key generation exposed eMudhra intermediate CA keys, letting attackers impersonate sites to non-browser TLS clients
threats.summary: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were incorrectly generated by the CA, so anyone can recover them from the certificates. Six are TLS intermediates trusted by the Chrome, Mozilla, Microsoft and Apple root programs, and two are codesigning intermediates trusted by Microsoft. An attacker with any of the keys could impersonate any website or service, and clients that ship their own CA bundle or do not enforce Certificate Transparency, such as curl, are most exposed.
actions: Update Python certifi to 2026.10.19 or later
Update curl CA bundle to 2026-10-20 or later
Update Homebrew ca-certificates to 2026-09-25_1 or later
Update Rust rustls-webpki to 0.103.16 or later
Update Rust webpki-roots / webpki-root-certs to 1.0.10 or later
Update Debian ca-certificates to 20250419~deb12u2, 20250419+deb13u1, 20260816+nmu1 or later
Update applications and libraries that ship their own CA bundle, including Electron apps.

action_quotes.quote: Users should update their browsers and operating systems to the latest versions as soon as possible.

action_quotes.action: Update applications and libraries that ship their own CA bundle, including Electron apps.
action_quotes.quote: These include applications and libraries that ship their own CA bundle, and apps built on Electron, such as Slack and Discord.

command-line tools that do not enforce CT

threats.title: MCP TypeScript SDK HTTP transports lack request limits
threats.headline: MCP TypeScript SDK servers over HTTP accepted unlimited bodies and batches, enabling unauthenticated denial of service
threats.summary: MCP servers built with the TypeScript SDK and reachable over HTTP put no limit on POST body size or on the number of messages in a JSON-RPC batch. Large requests could exhaust server memory, and one long batch could block the server from serving anyone else. No credentials were needed unless the application authenticates requests before they reach the SDK.
actions: Cap request body size in a reverse proxy until the SDK is upgraded.

action_quotes.action: Cap request body size in a reverse proxy until the SDK is upgraded.

threats.title: vLLM SHM multimodal cache allows forged handles to reach pickle
threats.headline: Authenticated vLLM callers can forge SHM cache handles to run arbitrary Python in worker processes.
threats.summary: When the SHM multimodal processor cache is enabled, vLLM treats an address and monotonic_id pair as authority to read shared memory in the worker. A caller can forge this pair through public HTTP routes so the worker unpickles attacker-staged bytes. This lets an ordinary authenticated inference caller execute arbitrary Python in the worker process, even with insecure serialization disabled.
actions: Check whether your deployments enable the SHM multimodal processor cache.

action_quotes.action: Check whether your deployments enable the SHM multimodal processor cache.
action_quotes.quote: When --mm-processor-cache-type shm is enabled, vLLM's multimodal SHM cache represents a cached item with an address and monotonic_id pair and treats that pair as authority to dereference shared memory in the worker.

who: vLLM deployments using SHM multimodal caching
threats.quote: An ordinary authenticated inference caller can execute arbitrary Python in the worker process on a deployment that uses SHM multimodal caching.

items.title: Shared agent skill files become a serving cost lever, not just a style guide
items.connection: HiCache turns repeated prompt prefixes into cache hits across parallel serving, and mattpocock/skills shows teams converging on shared skill files that every agent session loads first.
items.context: platform teams already standardize system prompts for coding agents they self-host
chain: Skill files are becoming a common way to package engineering practice, so many agent sessions start with the same long text.
HiCache reuses that prefix KV cache across context parallelism, pipeline parallelism, speculative decoding and disaggregated serving; on coding-agent traffic it lifted hit rate from 30% to 95%.
A platform team that freezes and orders skill files identically across teams makes that shared prefix stable, so more traffic lands in cache.
Skill governance moves from a developer-experience task to an infrastructure budget item, with a skills owner who tracks cache hit rate.
items.who: Platform and ML infra teams running self-hosted coding agents benefit. Engineering leadership pays through GPU budgets that go further.
items.variable: GPU cost per agent session and median time to first token
items.versus: Without a shared prefix discipline, each team's ad hoc prompts fragment the cache, and buying more GPUs costs more than reordering text files.
items.smallest_test: Replay one week of internal agent traffic through SGLang with HiCache, once with per-team prompts and once with a single ordered skills prefix; success is a hit-rate gain of 20 points or more.
items.disconfirm: Hit rate barely changes because user code context, not the skills prefix, dominates the shared tokens.

items.title: Self-hosted Git servers become the hidden bottleneck for persistent agent teams
items.connection: OpenRig wires Claude Code, Codex and Pi into persistent teams with owned work, and OpenAI's Pando account shows agent development volume forced a rebuild of a Git backend.
items.context: most enterprises run self-hosted Git and CI sized for human commit rates
chain: Persistent agent teams commit, branch and clone continuously instead of in human working hours.
OpenAI needed a new Git-compatible backend for Codex volume, a sign that ordinary Git servers strain under that pattern.
Enterprises adopting agent teams will see slow clones, CI queue backlogs and runner costs well before they see model bills grow.
Consultants can sell an agent-readiness audit of source control and CI, and Git hosting vendors gain a reason to sell agent-scale tiers.
items.who: Platform engineering and DevOps teams benefit. CTO budgets pay for capacity planning or consulting audits.
items.variable: CI queue time and clone latency per agent commit
items.versus: Waiting until the Git server degrades means outages that block human developers too, while load testing now is cheap.

items.title: AI buyers can prove a vendor never swapped in a quietly edited model
items.connection: heretic makes behavior edits to a model a quick step with no training, so silent swaps get easier, while FlashProve lets a provider commit to hidden weights and prove each reply came from that exact model.
items.context: regulated buyers already audit vendors by sampling rather than checking every transaction
chain: heretic lets anyone strip refusals or reduce sycophancy without fine-tuning, so a vendor's model can drift from what was evaluated with little cost or trace.
FlashProve binds replies to committed weights, and any heretic-style edit would no longer match the committed model.
Because proofs cost about 70 to 95 times the GPU time of plain inference, buyers write contracts that require proofs on a random sample of calls, not every call.
Model attestation becomes a procurement clause in banks, insurers and health systems, and vendors that can offer sampled proofs win audited deals.
items.who: Compliance and vendor-risk teams in finance and healthcare benefit. AI vendors selling to them pay for the extra proof compute and pass it into premium tiers.
items.variable: audit findings per AI vendor review
items.versus: Today buyers rely on vendor attestations and logs that cannot show which weights produced an answer, and no existing product proves this cryptographically.
items.smallest_test: Run FlashProve on a small open model, apply a heretic edit, and check that proofs from the edited model fail against the original commitment in 100% of 50 sampled replies, with CPU verification taking seconds.
items.disconfirm: Edited weights still pass verification against the original commitment, or proof cost on a production-size model is far above the 70 to 95 times range.
